channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Building an Autonomous Delivery Experience with DoorDash Co-Founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang
gist: DoorDash co-founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang detail how Ask DoorDash (conversational AI ordering) is unlocking latent restaurant-discovery and grocery-basket demand, and how eight years of quiet robotics experimentation produced DOT, a purpose-built 300lb/20mph autonomous delivery vehicle now running fully autonomous (L4) in Phoenix for over two years, with the founders arguing DoorDash's 10B-delivery operational data and 'use-case-first' philosophy are moats that generic robotics/AI-first approaches can't replicate.

insights.claim: DoorDash's conversational ordering feature drove 50% of restaurant-search trajectories to be orders from places customers had never ordered from before, a metric the company had historically struggled to move.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Suggests natural-language interfaces unlock latent restaurant-discovery demand that traditional search/keyword UX suppressed — a template other marketplaces (travel, retail) could copy to grow basket diversity.
insights.quote: we are seeing people 50% of trajectories of people using Ask Door Dash for restaurants... are people ordering from places they've never ordered from before, which is huge because that's one of the hardest metrics historically for Door Dash for us to move

insights.claim: On the grocery side, DoorDash is seeing roughly 40% larger basket sizes when customers use the Ask DoorDash conversational interface (e.g., photographing their fridge to restock, or planning a themed dinner) versus traditional tap-through ordering.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Basket-size expansion via conversational commerce is a direct GMV/revenue lever; investors should watch whether this trend persists at scale and whether it's copyable by Instacart/Amazon.
insights.quote: we're seeing a lot higher basket sizes, like I would say like 40% larger basket sizes on grocery

insights.claim: DoorDash originally bet on voice as the modality for AI-driven ordering a couple of years ago, but that approach did not gain traction; text/conversational chat interfaces succeeded instead.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete data point that voice-first AI commerce has repeatedly underdelivered versus chat/text interfaces — relevant to founders and investors betting on voice-agent startups.
insights.quote: it actually originally we were bullish on voice as the modality... that ended up not being the thing

insights.claim: Andy Fang observes there is now more agent traffic on the web than human traffic, and believes a DoorDash built from scratch today would be designed 'agentic-first' rather than as a human-browsing app.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A directional signal that commerce infrastructure (checkout, catalogs, APIs) should be redesigned for agent consumption, not just human UX — relevant for e-commerce infra investors.
insights.quote: there's more agent traffic on the web than human traffic, you know, and so it's like how do we have a Door Dash type experience that plays into that trend

insights.claim: DoorDash launched a CLI product that lets users/agents place orders programmatically; an early real-world use case had an office manager point a camera at a pantry shelf so an agent could auto-restock via DoorDash when supplies ran low.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates a concrete emerging pattern of 'ambient' agentic commerce (sensor-triggered reordering) that could expand DoorDash's grocery/retail TAM beyond on-demand meal delivery.
insights.quote: when the shelf starts to get empty, like I can fire off like a query to Door Dash to like stock up my shelf

insights.claim: Andy Fang notes that Google search queries have grown longer over the past couple of years, which he interprets as evidence people are increasingly comfortable conversing with apps/agents the way they would with a person — a trend he expects to reduce purchase friction across categories beyond food.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A leading indicator for any consumer product betting on conversational-first UX; longer queries imply users are ready for agent-native interfaces broadly, not just in food delivery.
insights.quote: one of the trends that I found fascinating is like over the past couple years, Google search query links have gone longer

insights.claim: DoorDash began exploring robotics and autonomy internally in 2018 — roughly 7-8 years before this conversation — starting as a 'skunkworks' project with one engineer and half of another's time, well before autonomy was an obvious bet.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Long-duration, low-cost internal R&D bets that predate market consensus can become durable competitive moats once the technology matures — a pattern investors can look for in other 'boring' incumbents.
insights.quote: we've actually been looking into robotics autonomy probably much longer than people thought, like since 2018 actually

insights.claim: Stanley Tang argues most autonomy/robotics startups build the technology first and retroactively search for a problem to fit it, the inverse of the software-world 'build something people want' discipline — and that this mismatch is why sidewalk robots (~2mph, short range) and robotaxis (4,000lb, built for people) both fail DoorDash's actual delivery use case.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A useful due-diligence heuristic for robotics investors: discount startups that lead with technology capability over a validated operational use case.
insights.quote: in in in software world like when went through YC like we're always taught to oh you got to serve the customer build something people want... but then when it comes to like hardware and hard tech and AI and and robotics, it's people just kind of do the opposite where they try to build the tech first

insights.claim: DoorDash's average delivery is 3-5 miles with a ~15 minute delivery window (excluding food prep time), which ruled out ~2mph sidewalk robots as too slow and 4,000lb robotaxis as unnecessarily large/expensive for carrying a few items — leading DoorDash to design DOT as a ~300lb, 20-25mph 'autonomous motorcycle/scooter' form factor instead.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Defines a specific, quantified product-market fit gap (weight/speed profile between sidewalk bots and robotaxis) that other delivery-robotics entrants would need to address to compete with DoorDash.
insights.quote: the average delivery at Door Dash is about 3 to 5 miles... If you put a 2 mile per hour sidewalk robot, it's just never going to work

insights.claim: Stanley Tang frames the hardest unsolved problem in delivery robotics as the 'first and last 100 feet' — pickup at the merchant and precise drop-off at a customer's specific door/gate/porch — which sidewalk robots and robotaxis (built for point-to-general-area, not exact-door delivery) don't solve.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Names a specific technical/operational bottleneck that investors evaluating any last-mile robotics startup should probe for — GPS pins are not precise enough for autonomous delivery.
insights.quote: what I call the first and last 100 feet problem

insights.claim: DOT, DoorDash's in-house autonomous delivery robot, weighs about 300 lbs, travels up to 20mph, is roughly one-tenth the size of a car, and is the only delivery robot designed to operate on sidewalks, bike lanes, and roads; it has been doing fully autonomous (L4) deliveries in Phoenix/Tempe for almost two years.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Concrete specs and operating history investors can use to benchmark DOT against competing last-mile robots (Nuro, Starship, Serve Robotics, etc.) on speed/range/autonomy-level.
insights.quote: It's uh weighs 300 lb, travels up to 20 mph. It's one tenth the size of a car... it's fully autonomous L4

insights.claim: Scaling DOT surfaced real-world edge cases invisible in demos: leaves partially covering a wheel path caused torque imbalance between wheels, hard braking triggered a regenerative-braking electric shock that overwhelmed the battery, and a hastily-built Jenkins boot-up script that took 30-45 minutes became a massive fleet-wide productivity bottleneck once scaled to hundreds of robots.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates why robotics scaling costs and timelines are systematically underestimated — a caution for investors pricing in fast fleet-scaling assumptions for any physical-AI company.
insights.quote: maybe half your wheels the right two wheels are on the leaves the left two wheels are still on the asphalt... the torque you have to send to the wheels is like very different

insights.claim: DoorDash partnered with 'Also,' a micromobility company spun out of Rivian (with Rivian's founder/CEO RJ Scaringe as board chairman), to solve hardware manufacturing/supply-chain/component-reliability problems once DOT needed to scale from ~100 hand-built robots to thousands.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete supply-chain partnership investors can track; signals hardware/manufacturing scale-up (not the autonomy algorithm) is now the binding constraint in delivery robotics.
insights.quote: we actually partnered up with this company called also which is this micromobility company that's spun out of Rivian... RJ is actually the board founder and chairman of the company

insights.claim: Stanley Tang argues that five years ago the binding constraint on delivery robotics was whether autonomy itself was even possible; today autonomy is increasingly a solved/less-constraining piece, and the real bottlenecks have shifted to operations/fleet-management (adapting to different city/restaurant behaviors) and hardware manufacturing/supply chain reliability at scale.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Reframes where value/risk sits in the delivery-robotics stack — investors should weight operations and manufacturing execution more heavily than autonomy-algorithm IP going forward.
insights.quote: the problem 5 years ago was autonomy. Now it's increasingly becoming more about operations, commercialization, hardware, manufacturing

insights.claim: DoorDash's stated approach across autonomy, robotics, and AI is to start every long-term bet as a cheap, small experiment (echoing its own founding as a Stanford dorm-room project, politely.com, with 8 PDF menus and a Google Voice number) rather than committing large capital upfront.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A repeatable capital-allocation heuristic (cheap experiments before big bets) that explains DoorDash's ability to sustain multi-year moonshots without major write-offs — a governance signal for investors.
insights.quote: Door Dash was a Stanford college like dorm room experiment. It started out as a website called politely.com with eight PDF menus and a Google voice phone number

insights.claim: DoorDash's historical drop-off location data (exactly where a human Dasher has left packages at a given address/apartment complex) is a proprietary dataset that doesn't exist in Google Maps or anywhere else, and is being used to solve the 'last 100 feet' problem for DOT.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete, hard-to-replicate data moat argument for DoorDash versus new entrants in delivery robotics — investors should distinguish genuine operational-data moats like this from superficial 'we have a customer database' claims.
insights.quote: we can see where people are actually dropping off the package... it's that first and last 100 ft problem... that data doesn't exist anywhere else. It doesn't exist in Google Maps. It only exists at on at Door Dash

insights.claim: The host (a No Priors co-host and investor in robotics startup 'Sunday') argues that surface-level 'incumbent data advantage' claims are often overstated because most historical enterprise data (e.g., customer records) has little bearing on what an agent/robot actually needs to accomplish a task.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A useful investor filter: when evaluating 'data moat' claims from incumbents, ask specifically whether the data maps to the exact task the AI/robot needs to perform, not just whether the data exists.
insights.quote: they'd be like ah like we have the I don't know customer records and database and I was like that actually has like very little to do with the thing we're trying to we could try to accomplish with an agent

insights.claim: The host cites a portfolio robotics company ('Sunday') where real-world deployment revealed unimaginable long-tail scenarios (e.g., a cat sitting in a dishwasher) that no engineer could have anticipated in simulation, reinforcing that only real-world operational data — not imagined edge cases — reveals the true distribution of physical-world problems.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Reinforces a thesis for robotics investing: prioritize teams with real deployed fleets generating real-world data over teams still simulating or demoing, since the long tail of physical-world edge cases can't be imagined in advance.
insights.quote: if we're trying to do the dishes, why is a cat in the dishwasher?... that's not something you're going to go imagine

insights.claim: Stanley Tang argues DoorDash's key advantage in robotics/AI is pairing 'world-class operational expertise' (fleet deployment, data annotation, merchant integration) with world-class technology, whereas many AI researchers are hesitant to take on or underestimate the operational complexity of deploying physical systems at scale.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Suggests the winning strategy in applied robotics may favor operationally mature incumbents partnering with AI talent over pure AI-research-driven robotics startups lacking operations depth.

insights.claim: DoorDash's internal AI/model spend grew roughly 20x from January to June (of the year discussed) before flatlining, as the company shifted from open-ended experimentation to actively managing ROI — including routing cheaper tasks to open-weight models to cut cost while preserving 'frontier-level' intelligence for harder tasks.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A rare disclosed internal AI-spend growth curve from a large enterprise; the flatlining-after-20x pattern is a useful benchmark for how enterprise AI capex trajectories may evolve elsewhere.
insights.quote: our spend in June went up like 20x versus what the spend was in January... we're seeing it flatline

insights.claim: DoorDash released an internal benchmark called Dashbench to measure how well different models/harnesses perform on coding tasks, explicitly to calculate ROI on AI spend rather than take vendor claims at face value.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Signals a broader enterprise trend of building internal, task-specific AI benchmarks rather than trusting public leaderboards — relevant for AI evaluation/observability tooling startups.
insights.quote: we announced a benchmark called Dashbench a couple weeks ago now that was mainly focused on our ability to figure out how well various models and harness performed on coding tasks

insights.claim: DoorDash found that frontier models often perform much worse on real enterprise accounting/analytics/finance data than teams initially report ('it works okay'), once tested on the messy real data versus a simplified or curated evaluation set — an unresolved question of whether the gap is a harness/tooling problem or a genuine model capability gap.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A caution against assuming frontier LLM benchmarks translate directly to enterprise back-office functions (finance, accounting) — investors in enterprise-AI-for-finance should probe real-data performance, not curated demos.
insights.quote: when we actually have it with the enterprise data with all the real stuff it's not performing as well

insights.claim: DoorDash acquired a company called Metis to help infuse 'AI-native' working practices into its 10,000+ person organization, and is seeing the fastest growth in AI tool adoption not in engineering but in non-technical functions like analysts and account managers automating tasks such as merchant QBRs.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Evidence that AI adoption inside large enterprises is beginning to shift from engineering-only gains toward broader operational/white-collar functions — relevant to enterprise AI-enablement vendors.
insights.quote: we're actually seeing the highest amount of growth in our organization in terms of like seats in the non-technical organizations

insights.claim: DoorDash currently has over 9 million Dashers doing deliveries and the business is growing 25% year-over-year; Andy Fang predicts DoorDash will have more human Dashers, not fewer, in 10 years because robotics/autonomy alone cannot supply enough delivery capacity for a business aiming to 5-10x from current scale.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A contrarian labor-market prediction: automation in delivery may expand total volume enough to grow human gig-work employment rather than shrink it — relevant to labor-market and gig-economy investment theses.
insights.quote: my prediction actually is in a world where robotics, drones, AI is is everywhere... we're actually going to have more Dashers doing doing deliveries, not less

insights.claim: DoorDash's stated strategy is a multimodal delivery fleet — DOT for dense-suburb 3-5 mile trips, drones for rural/low-infrastructure lightweight orders, and human Dashers for complex multi-step grocery orders requiring stairs/picking — rather than a single robot solving 100% of delivery use cases.
insights.speaker: Stanley Tang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: A capital-efficient product strategy (matching delivery modality to use case rather than betting everything on one robot form factor) that other logistics/delivery companies could replicate.
insights.quote: let's go with a how do you come up with a multimodal strategy where perhaps you know you have door dash Dot do kind of the 3 to five mile suburban deliveries

insights.claim: Andy Fang argues DoorDash's pitch to recruit scarce robotics/applied-AI talent is that engineers can ship real products used at scale in the physical world, rather than working on prototypes/demos in an academic-style lab — a differentiator versus researchers who have spent years without shipping.
insights.speaker: Andy Fang, DoorDash co-founder
insights.so_what: Talent-acquisition positioning that investors in robotics-adjacent companies should note as a competitive factor in the tight market for applied-robotics engineers.
insights.quote: do you want to go work on prototypes and demos and and do and be at a PhD lab or do you want to work on something where you can actually ship something in the real world
